answer.decision: Partition by account key with ordered processing per partition and dead-letter handling.
answer.action: Route every event by stable account ID and process each account’s monotonically increasing source sequence in order. Retry transient failures with bounded backoff, using account ID plus source sequence number as the idempotency key. When an event exceeds the retry or age threshold, quarantine it in a dead-letter queue and pause subsequent events only for that account while other accounts continue; alert operators and provide ordered replay after remediation. Load-test and provision sufficient partitions and consumers to sustain at least 20,000 events per second, with monitoring for hot accounts, sequence gaps, retry latency, and dead-letter backlog.
reasons: Account-key partitioning matches the required ordering scope while allowing independent accounts to execute concurrently.
A global FIFO design cannot meet the throughput requirement because the tested consumer group plateaued at 6,500 events per second.
Per-account source sequence numbers enable detection of gaps, duplicates, and out-of-order delivery.
Account ID plus source sequence number makes retries safe because downstream operations are idempotent for that pair.
Dead-letter quarantine with account-level pausing prevents a poison event from blocking all accounts without applying later events for the affected account out of source order.
The platform’s support for at least 256 key-ordered partitions provides substantial parallelism, subject to capacity validation.
Last-write-wins reconciliation cannot guarantee that every billing-state transition is applied in source order.
assumptions: A stable account ID is available for deterministic routing on every event.
The consumer architecture can isolate retries and pauses by account rather than blocking every account sharing a physical partition.
Dead-lettered events can be replayed together with held subsequent events in source-sequence order after remediation.
The required partition and consumer counts will be established through sustained load testing.
risks: High-volume accounts may become hot keys whose processing remains inherently serial and experiences elevated latency.
If retry isolation exists only at the physical-partition level, one poison account could block unrelated accounts mapped to that partition.
Incorrect sequence-gap handling or replay procedures could violate per-account ordering.
Poorly chosen retry thresholds could quarantine recoverable events prematurely or delay an affected account excessively.
Unresolved dead-letter events can leave an account’s billing state stale and build a growing held-event backlog.
Partition scaling or consumer failover may disrupt ordering unless the platform guarantee and consumer sequence checks cover those transitions.

citations.claim: Ordering is required within each account, while unrelated accounts are independent.
The design must sustain at least 20,000 events per second, while the tested single FIFO consumer group plateaued at 6,500 events per second.
A poison event must not block all accounts, and a previous poison event blocked its queue for 38 minutes.
The source provides per-account monotonic sequence numbers, and downstream operations are idempotent for account ID plus source sequence number.
Most accounts have low event rates, a small set is high-volume, and the platform supports at least 256 partitions with ordering by partition key.
